html:
A form of masked dance drama from Japan, shaped in the late 1300s and still performed today. It is the oldest major theatre art of Japan still regularly performed.

Noh grew from older temple and village shows. Its makers were the actor Kan'ami and his son Zeami. In 1374 the young shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu saw them perform at Kyoto and took the boy under his patronage. Zeami wrote many of the plays still staged and treatises on the art, built around yūgen, a quiet, deep beauty.

A noh play is slow and spare. A few actors move on a bare wooden stage with a painted pine tree at the back, to a chorus, flute and drums. The main actor often wears a carved wooden mask and plays a ghost, god or demon who tells the story of a past life, often from the Tale of Genji or the Heike wars. Comic kyōgen plays are shown between the noh pieces. Later popular theatre such as kabuki borrowed from it.
